source.title: 'Rarely' a problem? Language models exhibit inverse scaling in their predictions following 'few'-type quantifiers
source.authors: James A. Michaelov; Benjamin K. Bergen

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: It measures model performance on a task across model sizes, bearing on whether task performance improves with scale, but it measures quantifier prediction accuracy rather than the original claim’s held-out pretraining loss or compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The paper reports accuracy and sensitivity for 22 models in two experiments. Rows record the separately reported accuracy values relevant to V6. Sensitivity scores are reported too, but are omitted under the 60-row cap; the paper states they show no clear size pattern. The paired-stimulus design controls for differences in the unconditioned probability of the final words. Cited scaling results from other work are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: It measures accuracy on a quantifier-sensitive word-prediction task across 22 pretrained autoregressive LMs in five size series. Within each series, few-type accuracy mostly falls as size grows, which the authors present as inverse scaling. That directly bears on whether downstream performance improves predictably with scale (V6). It does not measure pretraining loss, fit power laws or study compute allocation.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors find all models poor on few-type quantifiers and generally worse with size, while most-type accuracy improves. They attribute this to rising typicality sensitivity with flat, low quantifier sensitivity. They argue larger models increasingly match human online (N400) predictions rather than offline judgements, even after instruction fine-tuning. They frame this as possible outer misalignment between probability and plausibility. They leave open whether the small uptick at the largest GPT-3 and InstructGPT models in Experiment 2 begins a U-shaped curve.
record.recipe_differences: This study evaluates surprisal-based critical-word prediction accuracy and sensitivity across model sizes; it does not measure held-out language-model loss, fit scaling laws, or optimize parameters and tokens under fixed compute.
record.method_sensitivity: The measured results differ between critical-word-only stimuli (Experiment 1) and stimuli with a following period (Experiment 2). The paper also reports local exceptions to the broad size trend, varying by model series.

fits_no_version.finding: Quantifier sensitivity (correct on both most and few) stays low (at most 7.5%) with no clear size trend.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Sensitivity to quantifier meaning does not scale with model size.

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: The stimuli are limited to those from one prior study. The authors could not test models larger than GPT-3 175B and note that some inverse-scaling patterns may become U-shaped at larger scales. Reported outcomes are accuracy and sensitivity on a specific quantifier task, not pretraining loss; no uncertainty estimates are stated.
record.rows_left_out: The Appendix A, Table 1 sensitivity values for all models in both experiments are omitted. The additional most-type accuracy values for GPT-2, GPT-3, InstructGPT, and OPT beyond the selected endpoints, and all GPT-Neo/GPT-J most-type accuracy values, are omitted to remain within 60 rows. The paper reports those values separately in Appendix A, Table 1.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss is measured or fitted against parameters, tokens or compute.
No extrapolation from small to large runs.
No shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
No other modality or training regime is fitted to a power law.
Relation of task performance to pretraining loss is not tested. No functional form or prediction of task accuracy is fitted.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents.

record.verdict_notes: Comparisons are within model series only, since series differ in training data. Accuracy is a binary pairwise surprisal comparison on 120 frames (240 pairs per quantifier type), with no uncertainty reported, so small step changes may be noise. Sizes reach only 175B; the authors flag possible U-shaped reversal at larger scales (Wei et al. 2022). The record's per-step states for few-type rows are acceptable as stated.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure held-out pretraining loss or fit loss scaling against parameters, tokens, or compute.
No loss predictions from small runs are compared with larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation between model parameters and training tokens is evaluated.
The study does not compare depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
No other modality or training regime is evaluated for the claimed power-law form.
Tests accuracy on the specific few-/most-type quantifier prediction task across model sizes; it does not test downstream performance broadly or its relationship to pretraining loss.
The study does not compare fitted scaling exponents or compute-optimal splits under different fitting choices, nor test loss-curve bending.

relationships.condition: Few-type quantifier accuracy, within each of the five model series, both experiments
relationships.reason: Few-type accuracy falls with size, with small local exceptions. GPT-3 E1 drops 0.092→0.038; InstructGPT E2 drops 0.242→0.112; OPT E1 drops 0.129→0.033 (E1/E2 -few rows). The authors call this inverse scaling.
relationships.display_finding: Accuracy generally fell with size, including GPT-3 experiment 1 from 0.092 to 0.038, InstructGPT experiment 2 from 0.242 to 0.112 and OPT experiment 1 from 0.129 to 0.033.

relationships.condition: Most-type quantifier accuracy, GPT-2, GPT-3, InstructGPT and OPT series, both experiments
relationships.reason: The largest model beats the smallest in every listed series. Examples: InstructGPT E2 0.775→0.963 and OPT E1 0.867→0.967 (the -most rows).
relationships.display_finding: The largest model outperformed the smallest in every series, including InstructGPT accuracy of 0.775→0.963 in the second experiment and OPT accuracy of 0.867→0.967 in the first.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: challenges
reader_labels.condition: few-type quantifiers, across the tested model series and both experiments
reader_labels.reason: The authors report generally poorer few-type accuracy as model size increases; most series show a decline, with some local exceptions. Rows E1-G2-117-few through E2-OPT-13-few document the separate scores.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: most-type quantifiers, represented by smallest and largest GPT-2, GPT-3, InstructGPT, and OPT models in each experiment
reader_labels.reason: Most-type accuracy is higher for the largest than the smallest model in each listed series and experiment; the paper describes this general improvement with size. The table gives selected endpoint scores.
